title: How did mechanical clocks change the day?
hook: In the Middle Ages, a summer hour was longer than a winter one.
summary: They replaced hours that stretched and shrank with the seasons with twenty-four equal hours, rung out from town towers from around 1300.
cardText: Before them, an hour was a twelfth of the daylight, so it was longer in summer than in winter. Tower clocks from around 1300 rang out equal hours, the kind we still use.

cardBlocks.text: Picture a summer’s day in medieval London. Daylight was split into twelve hours, and so was the night, so a daytime hour in June lasted far longer than one in December. Sundials and water clocks followed this rhythm with no trouble.

Around 1300 a new machine changed the rules: a falling weight, slowed down step by step by a rocking part called the verge and foliot. It was hard to adjust every day, so it simply counted twenty-four equal hours. In less than a century, clocks on church and city towers were ringing those hours across Europe.
Mechanical clocks, from around 1300, swapped hours that changed with the seasons for twenty-four equal hours, the ones we still use.

deepDiveBlocks.text: For most of the Middle Ages, an hour was not a fixed length of time. Daylight was divided into twelve parts and the night into twelve more, whatever the season. The most common timekeeper was the water clock, which let water drip at a steady rate into a vessel and was easy to adjust as the days grew longer or shorter.

The first mechanical clocks may have been alarms that rang a bell to wake monks for night prayers. The English word clock comes from the German Glocke, “bell”. A weight on a cord turned an axle as it fell, and the verge and foliot, a swinging bar, let it turn only in small, even steps. Early clocks had no hands or dial: they just struck the hours, and they could drift by half an hour a day.

Because the mechanism was hard to change daily, clocks counted the astronomers’ twenty-four equal hours, and that became everyone’s standard. They were placed high in towers, where the weight had room to fall and the bells reached the whole town. The oldest surviving clock in England, at Salisbury Cathedral, dates from 1386. Hourglasses seem to have spread with them: people turned the glass when the bell struck. Seasonal hours lingered for centuries, and some tower clocks showed both kinds, but the simpler equal hours won.

claims.text: In the Middle Ages, daylight and darkness were each divided into twelve hours, so the length of an hour changed through the year.

support.excerpt: The liturgical hours were not twenty-four fixed and equal periods of time like modern clock-hours, but dependent on the division of the daily periods of daylight and darkness each into twelve parts – measurements that, therefore, changed throughout the year.

If one uses a “variable hour” system, marking off twelve hours of light and twelve hours of darkness, a daylight hour in June in London is a great deal longer than a daylight hour in December in the same city.

claims.text: Most sundials divided daylight into twelve parts whatever its length, and water clocks, the most common timekeepers, could easily be adjusted to these changing hours.

support.excerpt: for most of the period those in use since antiquity divided daylight hours, regardless of their length, into twelve parts.
The most common form of timekeeper in antiquity and the early Middle Ages was a water clock, or clepsydra, which allows water to drip at a regular rate into a collection vessel.
Water clocks could easily be adjusted to allow for variable hours as the seasons changed.

claims.text: The mechanical clock appeared around 1300, driven by a falling weight and regulated by a mechanism called the verge and foliot.

support.excerpt: This shift began around 1300 with the invention of the verge and foliot, a mechanism that regulated the falling of a weight, pulled by gravity, that in turn drove the mechanism of a clock.
The first clocks that dispensed with water or another dripping fluid and used a mechanism made of gears and levers to mark the passage of timeappeared in the early fourteenth century.

claims.text: Mechanical clocks counted 24 equal hours whatever the season, because their mechanism was hard to readjust every day; this made the astronomers’ way of counting time the standard for everyone.

support.excerpt: the counting of the hours was done according to the astronomers’ system of twenty-four equal hours per day-night, regardless of the season.

it was quite difficult to readjust the foliot on a daily basis to make the clock speed up or slow down as the days grew shorter or longer. The clock, in other words, failed to keep time the way most people had kept time for centuries, and instead made the astronomers’ method of telling time the standard for everyone.

claims.text: In less than a century, weight-driven clocks spread to all the cities and most important towns of Europe, often high on church and city towers.

support.excerpt: In less than a century, weight-driven clocks spread to all the cities and most of the important towns of Europe.
clocks, conspicuously mounted on church and urban towers (where public sundials had been mounted) as a sign of pride, more and more frequently chimed out the equal hours.

claims.text: Clocks were placed high in towers because a longer fall of the weight meant less frequent winding, and from there their bells could be heard across a whole city.

support.excerpt: Because the further the weight had to fall, the less frequent the winding, verge-and-foliot clocks tended to be placed high up in towers – where their ringing could be heard by, and regulate, a whole city.

claims.text: The first mechanical clocks only struck the hours on a bell and had no hands or dial; they could be off by as much as half an hour a day.

support.excerpt: These early devices struck only the hours and did not have hands or a dial.
Their errors probably were as large as a half hour per day.

claims.text: The first mechanical clocks may have been built in monasteries as alarms that rang a bell to call the monks to prayer at night.

support.excerpt: the first such devices may have been invented and used in monasteries to toll a bell that called the monks to prayers.
the first mechanical clocks seem to have been developed as alarms to awaken the brethren for prayers in the night.

claims.text: The English word clock comes from the German Glocke, “bell”, and “o’clock” recalls telling time by the bell.

support.excerpt: The name clock derives from the German word Glocke (bell)
late medieval Europeans told time by the bell (the meaning of “o’clock” in English).

claims.text: Seasonal hours stayed in use for centuries, and some tower clocks showed them next to the equal hours, which eventually won because they were simpler.

support.excerpt: The seasonal hours continued to be used for centuries, and tower clocks used faces with eccentric gearing to show them along with the equal hours – though the latter, being simpler, eventually triumphed.

claims.text: The oldest surviving clock in England, at Salisbury Cathedral, dates from 1386.

support.excerpt: The oldest surviving clock in England is that at Salisbury Cathedral, which dates from 1386.

claims.text: No sandglass (hourglass) has been found from before the mechanical clock; people turned them when the bell struck the hour.

support.excerpt: Sandglasses could have been invented at any time, but none have been found that date before advent the mechanical clock in the fourteenth century. People turned their glasses when the bell sounded the start of an hour

claims.text: In a simple mechanical clock, a weight on a cord turns an axle as it falls, and the verge and foliot escapement lets the wheels turn only in small, even steps.

support.excerpt: A simple mechanical clock consists of a weight on a cord that is wrapped around an axle. As the weight is pulled downward by gravity, it turns the axle.
the verge allows the crown wheel to rotate only in small, even, methodical steps.
